task.description:
WF-03 Step 2 -- design the fix for ISS-0440. Produce a design artefact under lib/letflow/design/ (suggested iss440-handoff-status-enforcement.md). Design only, NO implementation code.

READ ISSUE-FIXER's Step 1 diagnosis FIRST (artifacts_in[0]). It did real empirical work and CORRECTED two facts ORCH supplied at Step 00 -- treat its findings as the evidence base, but per HANDOFF_PROTOCOL.md 1.1 verify what your design leans on.

THE ESTABLISHED EVIDENCE:
  - EIGHT occurrences, not seven (this run's own trigger is the 8th), across SEVEN DISTINCT ROLES (TEST-DESIGN-VALIDATOR, TEST-RUNNER x2, RELEASE-VALIDATOR, CODE-DESIGNER, SECURITY-REVIEWER, REVIEWER, ELIXIR-DEV), none repeating more than twice. This is SYSTEMIC, not a single-role problem -- a fix targeting one role's prompt cannot work.
  - ORCH has NEVER been the offender. Every violation was written by the COMPLETING agent at step completion. That asymmetry is load-bearing: it is why an ORCH-side check is an INDEPENDENT second reader rather than asking the error-prone party to self-check.
  - Bad-value vocabulary: DONE x4, PASS x2, COMPLETE x1, FAIL x1.
  - TIMING, corrected: the linter's 8.4s is the QUIET-HOST number. ISSUE-FIXER measured 74.7s once, under 3 concurrent erl processes from other worktrees on this same checkout. A 9-15x slowdown under contention IS the real operating condition on this workstation (multiple concurrent sessions are normal here). AC5 must be judged against the contended number, not the quiet one. ORCH independently confirms concurrent sessions are routine.
  - run(_args) at lint_handoffs.ex:233 ignores its arguments and always lints the full corpus. No single-file mode exists. Any per-dispatch or per-file gate needs one built.
  - ORCH independently scanned all 1899 handoff JSONs: ZERO bad string values present today. Every past occurrence was fixed. So this design is purely about PREVENTING RECURRENCE, not cleaning up existing debt -- do not design a corpus migration.
  - No prior issue (ISS-0190/0191/0196/0198/0203/0204/0262) rejected any of the four candidates, so none is foreclosed by a decision record.

THE AUTOFIX AMBIGUITY -- ISSUE-FIXER resolved this empirically and your design MUST respect the result. Every recoverable historical fix mapped PASS/COMPLETE/DONE -> COMPLETED with zero counterexamples. But the single historical top-level FAIL is squash-merged out of recoverable history, so whether it should have become FAILED (lifecycle) or COMPLETED (a finished step with a failing result) CANNOT be determined. Therefore: an autofix may handle {PASS, COMPLETE, DONE} -> COMPLETED, and MUST REFUSE -- not guess -- on FAIL. Silently converting a genuinely FAILED handoff to COMPLETED would corrupt the pipeline's own record of what happened, which is worse than the violation. If your design includes autofix, state this refusal behaviour explicitly and say what the refusal looks like to the caller.

THE PROPERTY THAT MUST HOLD -- this is the heart of the design. ISSUE-FIXER named it: the check must fire as a MECHANICAL CONSEQUENCE OF AN ACTION THE PIPELINE CANNOT AVOID TAKING, with ZERO agent decision about whether to run it. All six prior mitigations were prose asking someone to remember, and all six failed. Your design must state, explicitly, which unavoidable action its enforcement rides on, and why that action cannot be skipped. A design whose answer is 'the agent runs the linter' or 'ORCH remembers to check' is the seventh failed mitigation and will be rejected.
  ISSUE-FIXER's recommendation, which you may adopt, refine, or reject with reasoning: restricted autofix (handles 3 of the 4 bad values with no agent action, riding CI's existing unconditional gate) PLUS candidate (b) wired into ORCH's EXISTING commit-at-dispatch mechanism -- the same precedent shape as ISS-0196 / HANDOFF_PROTOCOL.md 1.3, which has held since it was adopted. That precedent matters: 1.3 works because committing the handoff is something ORCH already unavoidably does.

ASSESS THE HOOK OPTION HONESTLY. ISSUE-FIXER proved a .githooks/pre-push works mechanically but noted (i) an unconfigured host has ZERO protection, (ii) no existing check_* task verifies hook setup so one would have to be built, and (iii) such a task could only run inside mix letflow.check -- which already catches 100% of these at CI anyway, making the added task nearly circular. AC2 demands that an unconfigured host either still be protected or have its non-setup detected by an existing gate. If you propose the hook, answer AC2 head-on. If you reject it, say so and why -- rejecting a listed option with stated reasoning is a legitimate design outcome.

ADDRESS ALL FIVE ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA in docs/issues/ISS-0440.yaml explicitly, especially AC1 (the mechanism must catch a DELIBERATELY-INTRODUCED bad status BEFORE CI, demonstrated by a real run) -- state how a validator will demonstrate that, and AC5 (the cost question) against the CONTENDED timing.

SELF-REFERENTIAL OPPORTUNITY worth using: this run's own handoffs are written by the very agents that produce these violations, and are checked by the very linter being changed. Your design can specify that the fix be demonstrated against this run's own handoff files. A fix that cannot catch a violation planted in its own run's handoffs has not been shown to work.

Deliverable: the design document plus a complete handoff (artifacts_out naming the design path, next_action routing to CODE-DESIGN-VALIDATOR). Commit both to branch feature/WF03-ISS0440-20260903.
